proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), \(n>4r\), \(i\in I_n\), and \(w\in\{1,2\}\).  Couple the finite-volume wave to the restriction \(D^{(w)}|_{\Lambda_n}\) of the infinite assignment field, as prescribed by the buffered-restriction definition.  Since \(i\in I_n\),
\[
 \{i-r,\ldots,i+r\}\subseteq\Lambda_n. \tag{1}
\]
By score locality, the exposure and realized potential outcome entering \(Z_i^{(w)}\) are measurable functions only of \((U_j,D_j^{(w)})\) for the indices in (1).  The graph edge-range condition ensures that restricting the graph to \(\Lambda_n\) removes no neighbor of \(i\).  Thus the local exposure and outcome in the finite and infinite constructions agree under the restriction coupling.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), both constructions use the same product \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) law on the assignment coordinates in (1), so their conditional exposure propensities also agree.  Exposure positivity makes both IPW denominators at least \(\varepsilon>0\).  Consequently every factor in the two score formulas agrees, and
\[
 Z_{n,i}^{(w)}=Z_i^{(w)}\qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{2}
\]
Finally, \(\Lambda_n\setminus I_n\) consists of the \(r\) left-end sites and the \(r\) right-end sites.  Since \(|\Lambda_n|=n\) and the locality radius \(r\) is fixed,
\[
 \frac{|\Lambda_n\setminus I_n|}{|\Lambda_n|}
 =\frac{2r}{n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This proves both assertions.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  For either \(w\in\{1,2\}\), the score-decomposition definitions give
\[
 \xi_i^{(w)}+h_i=(Z_i^{(w)}-m_i)+(m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P})
 =Z_i^{(w)}-\tau_{\mathrm P}. \tag{1}
\]
The definition \(m_i=\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]\) implies
\(\mathbb E_P[\xi_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]=0\).  Because \(h_j\) is \(\mathcal F_U\)-measurable, the pull-out and tower properties of conditional expectation yield
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\xi_i^{(w)}h_j]
 =\mathbb E_P\!\left[h_j\mathbb E_P(\xi_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U)\right]=0. \tag{2}
\]
All terms are integrable by the following envelope calculation.  If \(e_1\ne e_0\), at most one of the two exposure indicators in the IPW bracket is one.  The outcome envelope and exposure positivity therefore give
\[
 |Z_i^{(w)}|
 \le \frac{|Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)|}{\min\{\pi_i(e_1),\pi_i(e_0)\}}
 \le \frac B\varepsilon=K \qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{3}
\]
If \(e_1=e_0\), the two terms in the bracket cancel and (3) is immediate.  In particular the scores, their conditional means, and all variables in (1)--(2) are square-integrable.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) and \(i,j\in\mathbb Z\).  The exact-score-split lemma gives \(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K\), so the products and conditional expectations below are integrable.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), the graph and the common no-carryover exposure and potential-outcome rules are fixed, and \(Z_i^{(w)}\) is a measurable function of the assignment field \(D^{(w)}\).  Conditional independence of the two assignment waves therefore gives conditional independence of \(Z_i^{(1)}\) and \(Z_j^{(2)}\), whether or not their within-wave neighborhoods overlap.  Since the two waves have the same conditional Bernoulli design,
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
  \mathbb E_P[Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =m_i m_j \qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{1}
\]
The iid-innovation condition and graph, exposure, and outcome equivariance make \((m_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) stationary.  Hence \(\mathbb E_Pm_i=\mathbb E_Pm_0=\tau_{\mathrm P}\), and \(h_i=m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P}\) is centered.  Taking expectations in (1), putting \(i=0\) and \(j=k\), and expanding \(m_i=\tau_{\mathrm P}+h_i\), we obtain
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[m_0m_k]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[h_0h_k]
 =\gamma_h(k). \tag{2}
\]
The causal target was defined independently as
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)\).  Summing (2) over that finite covariance-support set proves
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}
   \left\{\mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2\right\}.
\]
Thus the observed-law cross-wave moment identifies the already-defined causal functional; the equality is not imposed as a definition.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  By score locality, conditional expectation over the product Bernoulli assignments integrates a score depending only on \((U_j,D_j^{(w)})\) for \(i-r\le j\le i+r\).  Therefore \(m_i\), and hence \(h_i\), is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U_{i-r},\ldots,U_{i+r})\).  Equivariance and the iid innovation law make \((h_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) stationary, its definition makes it centered, and the score envelope makes it square-integrable.  Thus \(h_i\) is a centered \((2r+1)\)-block factor, and \(h_i\) and \(h_j\) are independent when \(|i-j|>2r\).

For \(M>2r\), stationarity, centering, and finite dependence give the exact covariance expansion
\[
 \frac1M\operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^M h_i\right)
 =\gamma_h(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{2r}\left(1-\frac{k}{M}\right)\gamma_h(k). \tag{1}
\]
Here \(\gamma_h(-k)=\gamma_h(k)\) follows from stationarity and commutativity of multiplication.  Letting \(M\to\infty\) in the finite sum on the right of (1) gives
\[
 \lim_{M\to\infty}\frac1M\operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^M h_i\right)
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)=\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}. \tag{2}
\]
Every variance on the left of (2) is nonnegative, whence \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge0\).

Apply the cited finite-block coboundary lemma to the reindexed block factor \(h_{i+r}\), whose input block is \((U_i,\ldots,U_{i+2r})\).  Its limiting variance is (2).  Since \(h_i\) is centered, the cited equivalence says exactly that \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\) if and only if there is a square-integrable \(2r\)-block factor
\[
 g_i=g(U_{i-r+1},\ldots,U_{i+r})
 \quad\text{such that}\quad
 h_i=g_i-g_{i-1}\qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{3}
\]
Under (3), finite telescoping gives
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_n}h_i
 =\sum_{i=r+1}^{n-r}(g_i-g_{i-1})
 =g_{n-r}-g_r,
 \qquad
 \frac1{N_n}\sum_{i\in I_n}h_i
 =\frac{g_{n-r}-g_r}{N_n}. \tag{4}
\]
For \(n>4r\), \(g_r\) is a function of \((U_1,\ldots,U_{2r})\), whereas \(g_{n-r}\) is a function of \((U_{n-2r+1},\ldots,U_n)\).  These innovation blocks are disjoint, so the endpoints are independent; stationarity gives each the law of \(g_0\).  Consequently \(g_{n-r}-g_r\) has, for every such \(n\), the law of \(g^\star-g_0\).  Equation (4) therefore implies
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_n}h_i\Rightarrow g^\star-g_0.
\]

Fix \(n>4r\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Apply the established fixed-footprint Cayley/F\o lner concentration theorem to the additive group \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\) with
\[
 A=\{-r,\ldots,r\},\qquad C=A-A=\{-2r,\ldots,2r\}.
\]
Then \(|A|=2r+1\), \(|C|=4r+1\), \(\Lambda=\Lambda_n\), and the theorem's interior and pair sets are \(I=I_n\) and \(J_k=J_{n,k}\).  Moreover
\[
 N=N_n=n-2r,\qquad
 \nu=\min_{|k|\le2r}N_{n,k}=n-4r>0,\qquad
 |\Lambda|=n. \tag{1}
\]
We verify its primitive premises.  Score locality says that the score at site \(i\) depends only on \((U_j,D_j^{(w)})\) for \(i-r\le j\le i+r\), and exposure and outcome equivariance give the same translated score rule at every site and in both waves.  The exact-score-split lemma and positivity give \(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K=B/\varepsilon<\infty\).  The wavewise Bernoulli condition makes the conditional law of each assignment wave the fixed product measure \(\mu_p\), independent of the value of \(U\), and cross-wave conditional independence factors the two conditional wave laws.  Thus, for cylinder events \(A_U,B_1,B_2\),
\[
 P\{U\in A_U,D^{(1)}\in B_1,D^{(2)}\in B_2\}
 =P(U\in A_U)\mu_p(B_1)\mu_p(B_2), \tag{2}
\]
so the iid innovation coordinates and the two assignment-coordinate families satisfy the independent-coordinate premise.  The buffered-coupling proposition identifies the finite scores on \(I_n\) with the local infinite scores.  Finally, cross-wave identification identifies the theorem's population covariance sum with the causal target \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\).

The generic centering allowance specializes, using (1), to
\[
 \frac{4|C|^2K^2}{N}
 =\frac{4(4r+1)^2K^2}{N_n}=b_n, \tag{3}
\]
and the generic deviation radius becomes
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,|A|\,|C|K^2}{\nu}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =\frac{\sqrt{48n}(2r+1)(4r+1)K^2}{n-4r}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =q_n(\delta). \tag{4}
\]
The established theorem, (3), and (4) give
\[
 P\!\left\{|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|
 >b_n+q_n(\delta)\right\}\le\delta. \tag{5}
\]
The right side and both allowances are law-independent over \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), so taking the supremum over \(P\) proves the stated uniform inequality.

For the prescribed finite check, take \(r=1\), \(n=5\), the deterministic line, \(E_i(d)=d_i\), \(p=1/2\), and \(Y_i(d)=Bd_i\).  Then \(N_n=3\), \(Z_i^{(w)}=2BD_i^{(w)}\), \(m_i=B\), \(h_i=0\), and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\).  Over each of the \(2^{10}\) two-wave assignment vectors, every lag-product average and the product of the wave means lies in \([0,4B^2]\), so \(|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}|\le20B^2\).  Since \(\varepsilon<1/2\), \(K=B/\varepsilon>2B\), and hence
\[
 b_n=\frac{4\cdot25K^2}{3}>\frac{400B^2}{3}>20B^2.
\]
Thus no enumerated assignment rejects at the theorem's threshold.  Cross-wave independence also gives \(\mathbb E_P\widehat\Omega_n^{12}=0\) in this constant-\(m_i\) example, consistently with (5).

Write \(F_n=\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\).  The Janson boundary proposition ensures \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge0\), so the displayed null and one-sided alternatives exhaust the relevant boundary directions.  If \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) satisfies \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\), rejection entails
\[
 |F_n-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|=|F_n|>b_n+q_n(\alpha)=t_n(\alpha).
\]
The uniform concentration theorem with \(\delta=\alpha\) gives \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=1)\le\alpha\), uniformly over the null.

Now suppose
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=2b_n+q_n(\alpha)+q_n(\beta)\).  On nonrejection, \(F_n\le b_n+q_n(\alpha)\), and therefore
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-F_n
 \ge \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-b_n-q_n(\alpha)
 \ge b_n+q_n(\beta). \tag{1}
\]
For every \(\beta'\in(\beta,1)\), the function \(q_n(\cdot)\) is strictly decreasing, so (1) implies
\[
 |F_n-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|>b_n+q_n(\beta').
\]
The concentration theorem at \(\delta=\beta'\) yields \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=0)\le\beta'\).  Letting \(\beta'\downarrow\beta\) proves \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=1)\ge1-\beta\), including equality at the stated separation boundary.

For fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\), the envelope \(K=B/\varepsilon\) is fixed and \(N_n=n-2r\).  Hence
\[
 b_n=O(n^{-1}),
 \qquad
 q_n(\delta)
 =\frac{\sqrt{48n}(2r+1)(4r+1)K^2}{n-4r}
   \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =O(n^{-1/2})
\]
for fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and consequently
\(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\).

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), put \(L=4r+1\), \(a_r=2r+1\), \(\ell=2r+1\), and let
\[
 M=N_{n,\ell}=n-4r-1>0. \tag{1}
\]
By the block-factor boundary proposition, \(h_i\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U_{i-r},\ldots,U_{i+r})\).  Thus \(h_i\) and \(h_j\) are independent when \(|i-j|>2r\).  They are centered, so
\[
 \mathbb E_P[h_i h_{i+\ell}]=0. \tag{2}
\]
Cross-wave identification, stationarity, and buffered coupling imply, for every \(|k|\le2r\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[
 \frac1{N_{n,k}}\sum_{i\in J_{n,k}}Z_{n,i}^{(1)}Z_{n,i+k}^{(2)}
 \right]
 =\mathbb E_P[m_0m_k]
 =\tau_{\mathrm P}^2+\gamma_h(k). \tag{3}
\]
The same calculation at lag \(\ell\), followed by (2), gives
\[
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[
 \frac1{N_{n,\ell}}\sum_{i\in J_{n,\ell}}Z_{n,i}^{(1)}Z_{n,i+\ell}^{(2)}
 \right]=\tau_{\mathrm P}^2. \tag{4}
\]
There are exactly \(L\) short lags.  Subtracting \(L\) copies of (4) from the sum of (3) over \(-2r\le k\le2r\) proves
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}]
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)
 =\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}. \tag{5}
\]

We next derive the finite-sample deviation bound from independent primitive coordinates.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), both assignment waves have the same fixed product Bernoulli law and are conditionally independent.  As in equation (2) of the uniform-concentration proof, this implies that
\[
 U_1,\ldots,U_n, D_1^{(1)},\ldots,D_n^{(1)},\ D_1^{(2)},\ldots,D_n^{(2)}
\]
are mutually independent.  By score locality, changing one environmental coordinate can change at most \(a_r\) retained scores in each wave, whereas changing one assignment coordinate can change at most \(a_r\) retained scores in its own wave.  The score envelope and buffered coupling give \(|Z_{n,i}^{(w)}|\le K\), so a changed product differs from its old value by at most \(2K^2\).

For a fixed short lag, one environmental coordinate can affect at most \(2a_r\) products.  Since \(N_{n,k}\ge n-4r=M+1\), the sum of the \(L\) short-lag averages changes by at most \(4a_rLK^2/(n-4r)\).  The lag-\(\ell\) average, including its multiplier \(L\), changes by at most \(4a_rLK^2/M\).  Thus the total environmental-coordinate oscillation is bounded by
\[
 4a_rLK^2\left\{\frac1{n-4r}+\frac1M\right\}
 \le\frac{8a_rLK^2}{M}. \tag{6}
\]
Changing one assignment coordinate affects only one factor and at most \(a_r\) products per lag, so its total oscillation is bounded by
\[
 2a_rLK^2\left\{\frac1{n-4r}+\frac1M\right\}
 \le\frac{4a_rLK^2}{M}. \tag{7}
\]
Set \(c=a_rLK^2/M\).  Summing the squared oscillation bounds in (6)--(7) over the \(n\) environmental and \(2n\) assignment coordinates gives
\[
 n(8c)^2+2n(4c)^2=96nc^2. \tag{8}
\]
The cited McDiarmid inequality, applied with arbitrarily small strict enlargements of these weak oscillation bounds and then taking the enlargement down to zero, yields
\[
 P\!\left\{\left|\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}
 -\mathbb E_P\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}\right|>t\right\}
 \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2}{48nc^2}\right\}. \tag{9}
\]
Substituting
\[
 t=\sqrt{48n}\,c\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =q_n^{\mathrm u}(\delta)
\]
into (9), and then using (5), proves the asserted concentration inequality.

Under \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\), rejection by
\(\mathbf 1\{\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}>q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)\}\)
implies the two-sided deviation in (9) at \(\delta=\alpha\), so size is at most \(\alpha\).  If
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)+q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta)\), nonrejection implies
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}\ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta)\).  For \(\beta'>\beta\), strict decrease of \(q_n^{\mathrm u}\) turns this into a deviation strictly larger than \(q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta')\); (9) bounds its probability by \(\beta'\).  Letting \(\beta'\downarrow\beta\) proves power at least \(1-\beta\).  Finally, for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\), the displayed formula for \(q_n^{\mathrm u}\) is \(O(n^{-1/2})\), and (5) shows that no sample-centering bias term is present.

We first establish the upper bound.  By the definition of the canonical full observation, there is a law-independent Borel map \(T_n\) satisfying \(W_n=T_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\): each score is obtained from the realized outcome, exposure indicators, and strictly positive known propensity coordinates.  Hence \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\), and therefore \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), is a common Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The two-wave size-and-separation theorem gives, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\alpha
 \quad\text{if }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[1-\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\beta
 \quad\text{if }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
The definition of the minimax radius therefore implies
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{1}
\]

For the converse, we construct an exact-local, causal-realizable submodel whose complete observed laws have common support.  Fix \(a\in(0,2B]\) and set \(b=a/2\), so \(0<b\le B\).  Let \(G\) be the deterministic nearest-neighbor line, let the innovations \(U_i\) be iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\), set
\[
 E_i(d,G)=
 \begin{cases}
 e_1,&d_i=1,\\
 e_0,&d_i=0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 C_i(d)=(d_i,d_{i+1})\in\mathcal C:=\{00,01,10,11\}, \tag{2}
\]
and use two conditionally independent iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment waves.  In the coordinate order \((00,01,10,11)\), define
\[
 \mathcal H_0
 =\{v\in\{-b,b\}^4:v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}=0\},
 \qquad
 v^+=(-b,-b,b,b),\qquad v^-=-v^+.
\]
The set \(\mathcal H_0\) has six elements.  Let \(Q_0\) be uniform on \(\mathcal H_0\), let \(Q_1=(\delta_{v^+}+\delta_{v^-})/2\), and, for \(0\le t<1\), put
\[
 Q_t=(1-t)Q_0+tQ_1. \tag{3}
\]
Partitioning \([0,1]\) into intervals of the finitely many probabilities in \(Q_t\) gives a measurable map \(F_t\) such that \(V_i=F_t(U_i)\) has law \(Q_t\), independently over sites.  Under the resulting law \(P_t\), use the common no-carryover potential-outcome schedule
\[
 Y_i(d;U,G)=V_{i,C_i(d)}. \tag{4}
\]
The deterministic line is shift equivariant and has edge range one.  The rules in (2) and (4) are shift equivariant and depend only on \((U_i,d_i,d_{i+1})\), which lies in the radius-\(r\) window because \(r\ge1\).  Also \(|Y_i|=b\le B\), and
\(\pi_i(e_1)=\pi_i(e_0)=1/2\ge\varepsilon\) because \(\varepsilon<1/2\).  Thus every primitive condition in the definition of \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) holds, so \(P_t\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).

For a realized schedule \(V_i=v\), averaging the IPW score over the four equiprobable local assignment cells gives
\[
 m_i
 =\mathbb E_{P_t}\!\left[
 Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=1)}{1/2}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=0)}{1/2}\right\}
 \middle|\mathcal F_U\right]
 =\frac{v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}}2. \tag{5}
\]
Consequently \(m_i=0\) on \(\mathcal H_0\), while (5) equals \(a\) at \(v^+\) and \(-a\) at \(v^-\).  Symmetry of \(Q_t\) gives \(\tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i=0\).  The schedules are iid over sites, so \(h_i=m_i\) is iid and
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i^2=a^2t,
 \qquad
 \gamma_h(k)=0\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_t)=a^2t. \tag{6}
\]
Thus \(P_0\) is a null law, and (5)--(6) verify that the moved parameter is the causal conditional exposure-effect variance.

It remains to bound the information in the complete observation.  Condition on both assignment arrays.  At site \(i\), the two observed outcomes select an ordered cell pair \((c,c')=(C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)}))\).  Let \(R_j^{c,c'}\) denote the law of \((V_{i,c},V_{i,c'})\) under \(Q_j\), and list probabilities in the atom order \((b,b),(b,-b),(-b,b),(-b,-b)\).  Exhaustive enumeration of the six schedules in \(\mathcal H_0\) and the two schedules \(v^+,v^-\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{ordered cell pair}&R_0^{c,c'}&R_1^{c,c'}\\ \hline
c=c'&(1/2,0,0,1/2)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\ne c'\text{ within }\{00,01\}\text{ or }\{10,11\}
 &(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\text{ and }c'\text{ in opposite exposure groups}
 &(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)&(0,1/2,1/2,0).
\end{array} \tag{7}
\]
The three rows cover all sixteen ordered pairs in \(\mathcal C^2\).  In each row every atom charged by \(R_1^{c,c'}\) has positive \(R_0^{c,c'}\)-probability.  Thus the raw two-wave outcome laws, unlike the latent four-cell schedule laws, have common support.  This table is also an exhaustive smallest-cell check of that claim.

Let \(R_t^{c,c'}=(1-t)R_0^{c,c'}+tR_1^{c,c'}\).  Direct substitution in (7) gives
\[
 \sum_x\frac{\{R_1^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}
 =2 \tag{8}
\]
for distinct cells, while the sum is zero for \(c=c'\).  For completeness, the elementary inequality \(\log u\le u-1\) follows because \(u-1-\log u\) has derivative \((u-1)/u\) and minimum zero at \(u=1\).  Applying it atomwise and using \(\sum_x(R_t(x)-R_0(x))=0\) yields
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{c,c'}\Vert R_0^{c,c'})
 \le \sum_x\frac{\{R_t^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}
 \le2t^2. \tag{9}
\]
Conditional on the assignments, the selected outcome pairs are independent over \(i\in I_n\), because the schedules \(V_i\) are independent.  The graph and assignment laws are identical under \(P_t\) and \(P_0\), and the exposures and propensity coordinates are deterministic functions of them.  Expanding the finite conditional product likelihood ratio and averaging over the common assignment law therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(\mathcal L_{P_t}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \middle\Vert\mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 =\mathbb E_D\sum_{i\in I_n}
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(
 R_t^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}
 \middle\Vert
 R_0^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}\right)
 \le2N_nt^2. \tag{10}
\]
This is a likelihood bound for the entire declared observation, not only for its score coordinates.

Put \(\eta=1-\alpha-\beta>0\) and choose
\[
 t_0=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2N_n}}.
\]
Because \(0<\eta<1\) and \(N_n\ge1\), we have \(0<t_0<1\), as required by (3).  The cited Pinsker inequality and (10) imply
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_{P_{t_0}}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}),
 \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 \le\sqrt{N_nt_0^2}=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}. \tag{11}
\]
Let \(\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) satisfy
\(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\le\alpha\).  To apply the cited binary two-point lemma to this randomized test, adjoin under both laws the same independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and reject exactly when \(A\le\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Direct integration of measurable sections shows that taking the product with this common uniform law preserves total variation.  The two-point lemma and (11) then give
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{t_0}}[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}
 =\beta+\eta\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)>\beta. \tag{12}
\]
By (6),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_{t_0})
 =\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{13}
\]
For every candidate separation not exceeding (13), \(P_{t_0}\) belongs to the corresponding alternative set and violates the required type-II bound in (12).  Taking the infimum in the definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) proves the lower bound.  Combining it with (1), choosing any fixed \(a\in(0,2B]\), using \(N_n=n-2r\), and using \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\) proves
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The assumption \(e_1\ne e_0\) is used in (2); if the labels coincide, the two IPW terms cancel identically.

The minimax-handle definition supplies a fixed Borel map \(T_n\) such that
\(W_n=T_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Every score test \(\psi_n\in\Psi_n\) therefore induces the full-observation test \(\psi_n\circ T_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\), with the same rejection probability under every \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Thus the score-test class is a subclass of the full-observation test class, and the two minimax definitions imply
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 \ge s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}. \tag{1}
\]
The full-observable minimax theorem consequently gives, for every \(0<a\le2B\),
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 \ge\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{2}
\]
For the upper bound, \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\) is itself a common Borel function of the score vector \(W_n\).  The uniform size-and-separation theorem therefore gives
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 \le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{3}
\]
The exactly unbiased proposition separately shows that
\(\mathbf 1\{\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}>q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)\}\)
is a common Borel score-vector test with level at most \(\alpha\), power at least \(1-\beta\) whenever
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 \ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)+q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta),
\]
and no sample-centering bias allowance.  Finally choose any fixed \(a\in(0,2B]\).  Since \(N_n=n-2r\), the right side of (2) is a positive constant times \(n^{-1/2}\), whereas (3) and the established formula for \(\rho_n\) give an \(O(n^{-1/2})\) upper bound for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\).  Hence
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
This conclusion concerns common Borel tests of \(W_n\); inequality (1) transfers the stronger full-observation converse to that restricted experiment.

Set \(r=1\).  Under each law in \(\operatorname{def:boundary-witnesses}\), the variables \((U_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) are independent Rademacher variables, so in particular
\[
 \mathbb E_P[U_i]=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[U_iU_j]=\mathbf 1\{i=j\}.
\]
The deterministic nearest-neighbor line is translation equivariant and every neighbor of \(i\) lies in \(\{i-1,i,i+1\}\), proving the graph-equivariance and graph-edge-range conditions.  For every fixed assignment \(d\), the pair consisting of exposure and outcome is measurable with respect to
\[
 \sigma(U_j,d_j:i-1\le j\le i+1),
\]
because the first schedule uses only \((U_{i-1},U_i,d_i)\), while the second uses only \((U_i,d_i)\).  Since \(|U_i|=1\) almost surely and \(d_i\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 |(U_i-U_{i-1})d_i|
 \le |U_i|+|U_{i-1}|=2\le B,
 \qquad
 |U_id_i|\le1\le B.
\]
Thus the support and locality requirements hold under the stated condition \(B\ge2\).

By the assignment part of \(\operatorname{def:boundary-witnesses}\), conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), the coordinates within each wave are independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) variables and the two waves are conditionally independent.  Because \(E_i(D^{(w)},G)=D_i^{(w)}\), the two relevant conditional exposure probabilities are
\[
 \pi_i(e_1)=P(D_i^{(w)}=1\mid\mathcal F_U)=p,
 \qquad
 \pi_i(e_0)=P(D_i^{(w)}=0\mid\mathcal F_U)=1-p.
\]
The primitive restriction \(p\in(0,1)\) makes both denominators positive, and the displayed hypothesis \(\varepsilon\le\min\{p,1-p\}\) proves exposure positivity.  This establishes every primitive listed in the narrowed statement.

For the remaining calculations, define the \(\mathcal F_U\)-measurable coefficients
\[
 A_i^{\Delta}=U_i-U_{i-1},
 \qquad
 A_i^+=U_i.
\]
Under the corresponding law the realized outcome is \(A_iD_i^{(w)}\).  Since \(e_1=1\), \(e_0=0\), \(D_i^{(w)}(1-D_i^{(w)})=0\), and \((D_i^{(w)})^2=D_i^{(w)}\), direct substitution into the defining exposure-IPW formula gives, for either coefficient \(A_i\in\{A_i^{\Delta},A_i^+\}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Z_i^{(w)}
 &=A_iD_i^{(w)}
   \left\{\frac{D_i^{(w)}}p-
   \frac{1-D_i^{(w)}}{1-p}\right\}\\
 &=A_i\frac{D_i^{(w)}}p.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This variable is bounded because \(|A_i|\le2\) and \(p>0\), so its conditional expectation exists.  Using the \(\mathcal F_U\)-measurability of \(A_i\) and \(\mathbb E_P[D_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]=p\),
\[
 m_i
 =\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =\frac{A_i}{p}\mathbb E_P[D_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =A_i.
\]

Under \(P^{\Delta}\), the Rademacher means yield
\[
 \tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P^{\Delta}}[m_0]
 =\mathbb E[U_0-U_{-1}]=0,
 \qquad
 h_i=m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P}=U_i-U_{i-1}.
\]
For every integer \(k\), expansion followed by the Rademacher covariance identity above gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \gamma_h(k)
 &=\mathbb E[(U_0-U_{-1})(U_k-U_{k-1})]\\
 &=2\mathbf 1\{k=0\}
   -\mathbf 1\{k=1\}
   -\mathbf 1\{k=-1\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
In particular, because \(r=1\) makes the defining covariance window \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2}^{2}\gamma_h(k)
 =2-1-1=0.
\]

Under \(P^+\), the same conditional-expectation calculation instead gives
\[
 \tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P^+}[U_0]=0,
 \qquad
 h_i=U_i.
\]
Independence and the Rademacher second moment imply
\[
 \gamma_h(k)=\mathbb E[U_0U_k]=\mathbf 1\{k=0\},
\]
and therefore
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2}^{2}\gamma_h(k)=1.
\]
These are exactly the two asserted population-variance values.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: If \(B\ge2\) and \(\varepsilon\le\min\{p,1-p\}\), then, with \(r=1\), the laws \(P^{\Delta}\) and \(P^+\) satisfy the iid-innovation, graph-equivariance, graph-edge-range, score-locality, outcome-envelope, wavewise-Bernoulli, cross-wave-independence, and exposure-positivity conditions listed in \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Under \(P^{\Delta}\), \(h_i=U_i-U_{i-1}\) and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\); under \(P^+\), \(h_i=U_i\) and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=1\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The frozen pointwise outcome-equivariance clause is incompatible with the constructed schedules under the declared left shift \((\theta u)_j=u_{j+1}\). For example, for the constant-one assignment under \(P^+\), it requires \(Y_{i+1}(\theta d;\theta U,\theta G)=Y_i(d;U,G)\), but the two sides are \(U_{i+2}\) and \(U_i\), which differ with positive probability under iid Rademacher innovations. Hence \(P^+\notin\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) as the class is written, so the original membership conclusion is false. The proposed claim removes only that conclusion and the unverified exposure/outcome equivariance clauses, while retaining every directly verified primitive and both exact covariance calculations.
